dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper studies how to best implement QAOA for portfolio optimization and related dense combinatorial problems on superconducting quantum processors that support two different CX implementations, termed bipotent architectures. The central framing is the trade-off between using higher-fidelity monolithic gates and exploiting pulse-level optimized primitives (such as ZZ and ZZ-SWAP) for dense instances like portfolio optimization and MaxCut, where many SWAPs are required.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The authors focus on QAOA for Portfolio Optimization and MaxCut with denser connectivity, and explicitly identify an algorithm-native gate set (ANGS) tailored to these QAOA variants, including H, ZZ, ZZ-SWAP, RZ, and RX. They introduce and analyze "bipotent" architectures where qubits have access to both direct-CX and ECR-CX gates, selectively optimize pulses only for frequently occurring primitives of QAOA using the ECR-based ZZ implementation, and exploit that ECR-CX enables pulse-level optimization without additional calibration.

dimension_3_key_results.text: Empirically, the authors find that on bipotent architectures the benefits of pulse-level optimizations currently outweigh those from vigorously optimized monolithic gates, and that the fidelity of circuit primitives alone is not always the best predictor of algorithmic performance; gate type and schedule duration also matter. They show that direct-CX gates have on average 4.82% lower error rates and 32.79% shorter gate times than ECR-CX, yet ECR-based, pulse-optimized ZZ and ZZ-SWAP (ZZOPT, ZZ-SWAPOPT) can deliver better overall performance, especially on dense QAOA instances where many SWAPs are needed. Bipotent circuits that combine direct-CX quality with ECR-based pulse optimizations can outperform mappings chosen purely on global fidelity, with ECR-ZZ-SWAPOPT and bipotent ZZ/ZZ-SWAP optimizations yielding the best and more stable approximation ratios (AR) and success probabilities (SP), including up to 70% AR improvement (29% on average) on portfolio optimization at depth p = 2. For MaxCut, they observe a size-dependent crossover where fidelity is more critical for medium-scale circuits while shorter schedule duration dominates for larger circuits, and combined ZZOPT/ZZ-SWAPOPT stabilizes AR and SP. Additional results highlight that qubit classes differ in decoherence properties, control-target polarity significantly affects quality, optimized ZZ has best QPT performance, and that decomposing ZZ-SWAP into CZ gates with polarity-aware pulse optimization gives the best ZZ-SWAP performance.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The codes provided do not report any explicit comparison to classical portfolio optimization or MaxCut solvers; performance is compared only across different quantum circuit and hardware configurations. Classical references, if any, are not captured in the available coding.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors explicitly limit their study to improvements that rely on existing calibration data and exclude any techniques requiring additional calibrations, which constrains the scope of achievable pulse-level optimizations. They also restrict pulse optimization to frequently occurring QAOA primitives to keep the approach tractable, implicitly limiting generality to those gate types.

dimension_6_future_work.text: Several future directions are outlined: adopting selective calibration that targets only specific two-qubit gates to reduce overhead; studying the noise resilience of different pulse shapes to find more robust pulses; extending the optimization techniques to other hardware architectures such as tunable couplers; leveraging dynamical decoupling in idle regions of shorter pulses for bipotent architectures; applying zero-noise extrapolation to suppress distinct error profiles of the two CX types; and developing universal, fully automatic methods to map arbitrary circuits onto bipotent QPUs.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The contribution is framed as introducing and analyzing bipotent architectures—devices with co-existing direct-CX and ECR-CX gates—and demonstrating that effective use of pulse-level optimized, algorithm-native primitives on such architectures requires explicit hardware–software co-design. The work highlights non-obvious factors such as control–target polarity and gate schedule duration in determining QAOA performance on dense portfolio optimization and MaxCut instances, and proposes bipotent qubit mappings that trade direct-CX fidelity against ECR-based pulse flexibility to improve algorithm-level metrics.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the study defines a clear bipotent mapping strategy that optimizes schedule duration while controlling fidelity, and evaluates four QAOA circuit families using multiple metrics: approximation ratio and success probability, plus schedule duration and CX count to capture circuit properties more fully than fidelity alone. The authors argue that control-target polarity of CX gates, typically ignored at the algorithm design level, significantly influences results, and emphasize that undirected logical gates like ZZ-SWAP should be implemented with attention to physical gate direction and timing asymmetries.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The paper reports that qubits connected to both CX types (Q-Bipotent) exhibit higher average T1 and T2 than qubits connected only to one CX type, which is a hardware characterization observation that underpins but does not directly fit into the other dimensions. It also stresses more generally that emerging bipotent architectures demand careful hardware–software co-design.
